questions.explain: The chapter states data egress fees, automated snapshot accumulation, and unmanaged log retention collectively account for 18–35% of total database spend, most of it recoverable.
options: 2–5% — negligible compared to compute
18–35% of total database spend for production workloads at scale
50–60% — hidden costs exceed compute
Under 1% if you use reserved instances
questions.q: What share of total database spend do data transfer, snapshots, and logs collectively represent?

questions.explain: The chapter warns that connecting via the public DNS endpoint incurs $0.02/GB cross-AZ charges even when both resources are in the same AZ — a single misconfiguration generating measurable egress on databases moving hundreds of GB/month.
options: It is free either way; endpoint choice does not affect billing
The private endpoint costs $0.02/GB; the public one is free
Using the public endpoint triggers $0.02/GB cross-AZ charges even when app and database are in the same AZ
The public endpoint doubles Multi-AZ standby costs
questions.q: Why does the chapter say endpoint choice (public vs private) matters for RDS data transfer costs?

questions.explain: A 500 GB database with 35-day retention holds ~17,000 GB of snapshots beyond the free 500 GB (first copy free), costing 17,000 × $0.095 = $1,615/month; retention cost scales linearly, so 35→7 days cuts ~80%.
options: A 500 GB database with 35-day retention stores ~17,000 GB beyond the free tier, costing ~$1,615/month — and retention cost scales linearly
Snapshots are free on AWS up to 35 days of retention
Snapshot cost is fixed per instance regardless of retention period
AWS charges $0.095/GB only for manual snapshots, never automated ones
questions.q: How does AWS price automated snapshots, and what is the chapter's illustrative 500 GB / 35-day example?

questions.explain: General query logging on a 5,000-qps OLTP database generates ~2 GB/hour → 1,440 GB/month → $720/month CloudWatch ingestion plus $43.20 storage = $763.20/month; slow query logging at ~1% of the volume satisfies the debugging need.
options: Audit logging — always the most expensive
Error log exports — they cannot be filtered
Slow query logging at a 100ms threshold
General query logging on high-throughput OLTP — ~$763/month on one database, replaceable by slow query logging at ~1% of the volume
questions.q: What is the single most expensive logging misconfiguration, and what replaces it?

questions.explain: The four-week sequence runs audit/baseline (week 1) → zero-risk retention/log-policy fixes (week 2) → log export and diagnostic changes (week 3) → traffic routing (week 4); weeks 2 and 3 each deliver 30–40% of recoverable savings, and all four weeks typically recover 70–85%.
options: Traffic routing first, then snapshots, then logs, then baseline
Week 1 audit/baseline → Week 2 zero-risk retention fixes → Week 3 log export changes → Week 4 traffic routing; all four weeks recover 70–85% of the opportunity
All changes in one maintenance window, ordered by cost impact
Logs first, then transfer, then snapshots; baseline is optional
questions.q: What is the chapter's four-week remediation sequence, and what does it typically recover?
